title: Eager sync vs deferred all-reduce trials
content:
Summary:

Quick experiment log comparing two communication coordination strategies for multi-GPU LLM inference stacks: (1) eager synchronous all-reduce semantics (aggressive, tight sync points) vs (2) deferred/coalesced all-reduce (buffered, combined across micro-batches/inflight requests). Goal was to quantify tail-latency, CPU/GPU overlap, and interconnect utilization under realistic inference traffic (peaky short sequences + occasional long sequences).

Motivation / Why we ran this:
- We see recurrent 95/99p tail spikes in serving clusters during mixed short/long token mixes. Hypothesis: conservative eager synchronization (we force all-reduces at layer boundaries per micro-batch) causes underutilized overlap and amplifies microburst sensitivity on NVLink/PCIe.
- Deferred/coalesced strategy may increase per-request variance but reduce system-wide contention by smoothing collective start times and enabling better kernel overlap.

Hypotheses tested:
- H1: Deferred/coalesced all-reduce reduces p99 latency under peaky traffic by ~15-30% vs eager sync when NVLink links are saturated.
- H2: Eager sync gives slightly better median latency for uniform workloads but suffers larger variance under contention.
- H3: Kernel overlap (compute+comm) is higher with deferred strategy, observable via Nsight timelines and nvlink/util counters.

Testbed:
- Hardware: 8x A100 (40GB) per node, 2 nodes connected by NVSwitch (DGX-like) and separate test on 8x A100 across two p4d.24xlarge instances (AWS) connected via EFA/NVLink (multi-node).
- Software: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8, NCCL 2.16, PyTorch 1.13 (runtime harness), custom serving runtime branch (github PR 412) implementing deferred-coalesce transport.
- Model: 13B decoder-only transformer. Sharding: TP=2, PP=4 (4 pipeline stages), model-parallel KV cache enabled.
- Workload generator: synthetic reproduced production mix — 70% short (max 32 tokens), 25% mid (128 tokens), 5% long (1024 tokens); QPS varied 50–500 to create microbursts.

Methodology / what we changed:
- Eager sync baseline: baseline runtime triggers all-reduce at each pipeline boundary and after layerwise sharded matmul gradients (inference-mode analog for KV/replica syncs). Micro-batches not coalesced.
- Deferred/coalesced: modified comm scheduler to hold small all-reduce ops for up to 1.5ms (config knob) and coalesce compatible ops across inflight requests and adjacent layers when safe (comm-only ops that do not change program semantics for inference). Also allowed opportunistic async launch of NCCL all-reduce but block completion only at commit points.
- Instrumentation: perf samples, nvprof/nvtx traces, Nsight Systems timelines, /proc/net/dev for host NIC, nvidia-smi dmon, NVLink utilization via `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=...` counters, and per-request tracing in the serving runtime (token timestamps). Microbenchmarks with oom/kick scenarios included.

Key results (aggregate):
- Median per-token latency: eager 11.8ms, deferred 12.6ms (deferred median slightly worse ~7%).
- p95: eager 34.2ms, deferred 27.9ms (deferred ~18% better).
- p99: eager 152.1ms, deferred 106.4ms (deferred ~30% better).
- Under extreme microburst (QPS=500), eager saw multiple 400–800ms tail spikes; deferred capped at ~220–280ms.
- GPU kernel overlap: Nsight timelines show >25% more overlap (compute kernels concurrent with reduction kernels) in deferred runs.
- Link utilization: eager produced sharper NVLink utilization peaks (short high amplitude) while deferred smoothed peak-to-mean ratio by ~3x.
- PCIe reads (host staging): eager had 1.4x more host-GPU transfers on average due to earlier host staging and repeated small transfers; deferred coalescing reduced transfer amplification.

Notable traces / observations:
- Example trace RW-E-20250210-01: eager run at 300 QPS — observed cascade effect: one stage stalls on all-reduce, downstream pipeline backpressure causes host staging queue to grow and then microburst of PCIe reads, amplifying tail.
- Trace RW-D-20250212-03 (deferred): all-reduce starts shifted to align with natural compute slack; small deferred waits (0.8–1.2ms) were often fully hidden by preceding matmul compute on fellow GPUs.
- NCCL behavior: with eager sync, NCCL launches many small collectives leading to higher packetization overhead and next-hop CPU interrupt rate observed on host; deferred coalescing led to fewer, larger collectives — better utilization of ring bandwidth.
- Unexpected: in some topologies (heterogeneous interconnect, mixed NVLink+PCIe paths) deferred coalescing created unfavorable alignments that routed collectives across cross-node links more frequently. This worsened tails in those specific layouts.

Micro-config sensitivity:
- Coalesce-window: 0.5ms -> less impact (closer to eager), 1.5ms -> best smoothing vs latency tradeoff in our tests, 5ms -> some requests saw increased median latency without additional smoothing benefits.
- Max coalesce size: combining >4 micro-ops introduced edge-cases where synchronization semantics (KV cache race) had to be carefully validated; we added correctness asserts for reordering safety.
- Pipeline stage imbalance: deferred helps when compute load per stage is balanced; when stage imbalance exists, deferred can worsen p95 because delayed collectives pile up on slowest stage.

Representative commands / repro notes:
- Baseline run (eager): 
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 python run_infer.py --tp=2 --pp=4 --coalesce_window_ms=0 --qps=300 --workload=mix_production

- Deferred run: 
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 python run_infer.py --tp=2 --pp=4 --coalesce_window_ms=1.5 --qps=300 --workload=mix_production --defer_allreduce=1

- Collect traces: Nsight Systems: `nsys profile -o trace_deferred --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt python run_infer.py ...`

Open questions / risks / TODOs:
- Risk: correctness for some custom fused kernels — need more fuzzing/validation to ensure deferred reordering not violating KV cache assumptions for inference with stateful hooks.
- Need to test at larger scale (16+ nodes) to validate cross-node routing effects. Some topologies we tried (AWS p4d multi-instance) showed cases where deferred worsened tails — need topology-aware coalescing heuristics.
- Investigate hybrid policy: eager for long-seq requests and deferred for short-seq bursts; run classifier + policy in front of comm scheduler.
- Evaluate interaction with the runtime's automatic batching and prefix-caching (deferred might be redundant with prefix cache replay path).

Next steps / action items:
- Jonah: add topology-awareness to coalescer (ticket RW-2189).
- María: run correctness fuzzing across fused kernels and KV-cache heavy workloads (RW-2190).
- Ethan: schedule 16-node run on on-prem cluster, capture cross-node NVSwitch traces (RW-2191).
- Aisha: draft an experimental playbook summarizing knobs and recommended defaults for hosted vs dedicated deployments; propose default coalesce_window_ms=1.0ms for hosted with balanced stages.

Notes & references:
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime -> link pinned (internal)
- Related experiments: see PR notes in github: serv-runtime PR 412 (deferred-coalesce prototype)
- Observability: add a per-collective id and latency histogram to console dashboards to make this behavior visible per-tenant.

Rough verdict (working draft):
- Deferred/coalesced all-reduce is a promising lever to reduce 95/99 tail spikes for peaky production-like traffic at our typical node sizes and NVLink topologies. Tradeoff is small median increase and topology sensitivity. We should iterate on topology-aware heuristics and a hybrid policy that uses request-length signals.

Raw metrics and traces are in: s3://redwood-experiments/runs/2025-02-eager-deferred/ (labels and trace ids in linked_artifacts).

Unresolved items to discuss in followup meeting:
- Should coalescing be enabled by default in hosted API? (ops implications, cost/latency SLAs)
- How to signal per-tenant policies and surface them in Console?

End of notes.
